articles.title: Association between multiday emergency department boarding and higher in-hospital mortality: evidence from Brazil.
articles.journal: European journal of emergency medicine : official journal of the European Society for Emergency Medicine
articles.abstract: Emergency department (ED) boarding is a major driver of overcrowding and has been associated with adverse outcomes. However, little is known about the impact of multiday boarding delays, which are common in low- and middle-income countries. Retrospective cohort study using administrative hospital data aimed to examine the association between ED boarding time and in-hospital mortality. Adult patients admitted via the ED of Hospital de Clínicas de Porto Alegre, a large tertiary hospital in Brazil, between January 2022 and December 2023. ED boarding time, defined as the interval between the admission decision and the patient's physical departure from the ED. In-hospital mortality was evaluated using multivariable logistic regression with restricted cubic splines modeling boarding time as a continuous exposure, adjusting for age, sex, and triage acuity. Among 28 743 admissions, the median boarding time was 1.8 days (interquartile ranges 0.6-3.5). In-hospital mortality was 8.36%. Compared with patients in the first boarding quartile (median 0.19 days), those in the last quartile (median 4.92 days) had higher adjusted odds of death [odds ratio (OR) 1.15; 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.05-1.25]. At the cohort median (1.8 days), each additional day of boarding was associated with a 6% increase in the odds of in-hospital death (OR 1.06; 95% CI 1.02-1.09). Prolonged ED boarding time was independently associated with increased in-hospital mortality, with no evidence of a safe threshold. Multiday delays represent a modifiable risk factor associated with excess mortality.

articles.title: Backcountry Risk-Taking (BRiT)-An Instrument to Evaluate an Individual's Overall Risk-Taking Behavior Within the Backcountry Avalanche Environment.
articles.abstract: Study HypothesisThe primary objective of this study was to develop and evaluate a novel instrument called the Backcountry Risk-Taking Instrument (BRiT) to measure risk-taking behavior among backcountry users. We aimed to create an instrument that is content-valid, grounded in theory, and psychometrically sound.MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional study to evaluate the psychometric properties of the instrument. Participants completed the newly developed 13-item instrument along with established measures of risk-taking behavior and risk preference to assess convergent validity.ResultsA total of 361 participants completed the survey. After listwise deletion, n = 280 were retained for factor analysis and n = 354 for convergent validity. The resulting instrument provides a concise, empirically supported framework for measuring backcountry risk behavior and establishes a foundation for prospective validation in future cohorts.ConclusionsThe BRiT instrument significantly advances avalanche risk assessment. BRiT demonstrates a clear and stable foundation built upon 3 domains: Core Gear, Avalanche History, and Terrain Choice. Continued validation and refinement across broader populations will strengthen its utility as a foundational tool for both research and applied avalanche risk management.

articles.title: Ambient Heat Exposure Is Not Associated with Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction among Emergency Department Patients with Acute Chest Pain.
articles.abstract: BackgroundHeat exposure increases cardiovascular risk, but its relationship with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) in emergency department (ED) patients is unknown. This study examined whether heat exposure increases NSTEMI risk in ED patients with chest pain.MethodsThis observational cohort study of adults with chest pain from 5 US EDs (April 1, 2019-October 31, 2023) used the Wake Forest Chest Pain Registry. Heat data were collected from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Heat exposure was defined as maximum daily heat index ≥80°F, the National Weather Service's cautionary threshold. The primary outcome was index NSTEMI, determined using validated diagnosis codes. Logistic models assessed the association between heat and NSTEMI. Multivariable models were adjusted for common cardiovascular confounders, and pollution-given its potential to exacerbate cardiovascular disease. Lagged analysis evaluated heat exposure over 5-d lags. Unadjusted and adjusted odds ratios (aORs) are reported with 95% confidence intervals.ResultsAmong 21,367 patients with chest pain, 52.7% (11,260/21,367) were female, the median age was 53.5 y (IQR 40-65), and 63.1% (13,486/21,367) had heat-exposed days. Index NSTEMI occurred in 5.9% of patients. NSTEMI rates were similar between those with and without heat exposure (5.8% [778/13,486] vs 6.2% [487/7881]; OR: 0.93, 95% CI 0.83-1.05). After adjustment, heat exposure remained unassociated with index NSTEMI (aOR: 0.91, 95% CI 0.80-1.03). Lagged analysis showed no association between NSTEMI and heat exposure in unadjusted (OR: 0.92, 95% CI 0.82-1.04) or adjusted (aOR: 0.94, 95% CI 0.82-1.07) models.ConclusionHeat exposure was not associated with NSTEMI in chest pain ED patients.

articles.title: Comparing Internal Self-Assessment and External Evaluation of Hospital Safety Index (HSI) for Disaster Response: A Cross-Sectional Study.
articles.abstract: Hospitals must ensure preparedness and safety to maintain services during disasters. Results from the Hospital Safety Index (HSI) often indicate that hospitals are safe and capable; however, it is important to verify whether these assessments are consistent across different evaluators. This study compared hospital safety scores between internal evaluators (hospital staff) and external evaluators. This cross-sectional study was conducted in 2022 using documented hospital safety assessment data from hospitals supervised by Kermanshah University of Medical Sciences (KUMS) in western Iran. Independent-samples t-tests, the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), and Bland-Altman plots were used to compare mean scores and assess agreement between evaluators. For structural safety, the difference between internal and external evaluators was not significant (95% CI, -9.19 to 9.67). In contrast, the differences were pronounced for non-structural safety (95% CI, 7.00 to 20.63) and functional safety (95% CI, 10.56 to 28.84), with both confidence intervals excluding zero. Agreement between evaluators was poor across most hospital safety domains (ICC < 0.05). Internal evaluators rated their hospitals significantly safer than external evaluators did. Given the pronounced differences in non-structural and functional safety, and the poor inter-rater agreement across most domains, relying solely on internal assessments may mislead hospital managers about disaster preparedness. Hospital managers should therefore regard external evaluation as an opportunity to reveal their hospital's vulnerabilities in disaster safety.

articles.title: Addition of a McLaughlin cerclage to locking plate fixation of distal patellar pole fractures reduces interfragmentary displacement - a biomechanical human cadaveric study.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: To investigate whether the addition of a McLaughlin cerclage to locking plate fixation of distal patellar pole fractures provides improved biomechanical construct stability and reduced interfragmentary displacement. A distal patellar pole fracture was simulated in sixteen fresh-frozen human cadaveric knees by a horizontal osteotomy in the distal third of the patella. Subsequently, locking plate fixation was performed. In a randomized half of the specimens, an additional McLaughlin wire cerclage was applied. The specimens were then subjected to 3000 cycles of extension starting at 90° of flexion under a maximum tensile load of 320 N. Using a Digital Image Correlation (DIC) system, the interfragmentary displacement between the proximal and distal fragments was measured at 1, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, 500, 1000, 2000, and 3000 cycles. Statistical analysis was performed using repeated-measures ANOVA and Welch's unpaired t-t test at 3000 cycles. An additional McLaughlin cerclage significantly reduced interfragmentary displacement under cyclic loading in comparison to locking plate fixation alone. After 3000 cycles, displacement was 2.27 ± 1.84 mm with plate fixation alone and 0.36 ± 0.22 mm with additional McLaughlin cerclage (mean difference 1.91 mm; 95% CI 0.38-3.45 mm; p = 0.0215). An additional McLaughlin cerclage reduced interfragmentary displacement in distal patellar pole fractures. In cases of unstable distal pole patella fractures, the additional use of a McLaughlin cerclage may therefore be considered to enhance construct stability.

articles.title: Trauma care performance and patient outcomes - insights from a major trauma centre in Sweden.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Trauma is a leading cause of death among individuals under 45 years of age. Evaluating trauma system performance over time is important but inherently difficult due to concurrent changes in patient demographics, case-mix and care processes. The aim of this study was to describe temporal changes in patient demographics, injury severity and trauma care at a major trauma centre in Sweden from 2017 to 2023. We hypothesised that risk-adjusted 30-day mortality decreased and that time to computed tomography was reduced over the study period. A retrospective cohort study was conducted using data from the Karolinska Trauma Registry, including all trauma patients aged > 15 years fulfilling criteria for full trauma team activation, admitted between January 2017 and August 2023. Multivariable logistic regression was used to assess changes in 30-day mortality over time, adjusted for age, sex, injury severity category, ASA score and injury type. Time from arrival to computed tomography was analysed by linear regression and, because the distribution was skewed, by quantile (median) regression. A total of 5,615 trauma patients were included. Over the study period, the patient population became older, and ASA scores increased, while injury severity and the proportion of penetrating injury remained unchanged. In multivariable logistic regression with 2017 as reference, the odds of 30-day mortality in 2022-2023 were lower (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.43-0.88, P = 0.008) after adjusting for confounders. Median time to computed tomography decreased from 31 to 21 min; the adjusted difference in 2022-2023 compared with 2017 was - 7.5 min by linear regression (P = 0.014) and - 10.4 min by quantile regression (95% CI - 11.5 to - 9.2, P < 0.001). Our findings are consistent with improvements in trauma care within a mature trauma system, with shorter median time to computed tomography and lower 30-day mortality despite an aging population with increasing comorbidity. However, the specific drivers of these changes are difficult to identify, and future studies should explore how individual components of pre-hospital and in-hospital care contribute to trauma outcomes.

articles.title: Quantifying Biomechanical Demand During Manual Overboard Rescue: Scenario-Based Application of the Revised NIOSH Lifting Equation.
articles.abstract: BackgroundMaritime first responders frequently perform manual overboard lifting during rescue operations, placing them at high risk for musculoskeletal injury, particularly in the lumbar spine. Conventional ergonomic guidelines, including the Revised National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) Lifting Equation (RNLE), were developed for controlled, symmetrical lifting and do not adequately capture the biomechanical and environmental demands of overboard recovery.PurposeThis study aimed to quantify biomechanical demand during overboard lifting from vessels with 1.8- to 3.0-m freeboard and to evaluate injury risk under conditions exceeding standard RNLE assumptions.MethodsThe RNLE was adapted to estimate Recommended Weight Limit (RWL) and Lifting Index (LI) for overboard lifting tasks. Scenario-based analyses examined object masses (0-140 kg), horizontal reaches (25-50 cm), and vertical lifting distances (0-175 cm). LI values were calculated at both lift origin and destination to capture phase-specific biomechanical risk.ResultsUnder idealized conditions, LI exceeded the recommended safety threshold (LI > 1) at loads as low as 15.6 kg for a horizontal reach of 25 cm. For a human-sized load of 90 kg, LI ranged from 3.9 to 7.8 depending on horizontal reach and vertical displacement, indicating substantial biomechanical overload. Increasing horizontal reach from 25 to 50 cm increased LI by 40 to 60% across all load conditions. LI exceeded 1 at both the lift origin and destination for all modeled loads ≥20 kg and vertical displacements ≥50 cm, highlighting the elevated risk inherent in these tasks.ConclusionManual overboard lifting imposes significant biomechanical strain that frequently exceeds conventional ergonomic limits. Task-specific metrics derived here provide quantitative guidance for injury prevention, including pre-employment functional screening, progressive task-specific conditioning, and the use of mechanical assistive devices. These findings support evidence-based occupational health strategies for maritime first responders and other personnel performing high-risk lifting tasks in dynamic environments.

articles.title: The Continuing Evolution of the International Diploma in Mountain Medicine: Balancing Global Standards and Local Context.
Physiological monitoring and physiology-informed strategies in cardiac arrest: current evidence and clinical translation.
articles.abstract: Despite advances in cardiac arrest management, survival with favorable neurological outcomes remains limited. Physiological monitoring may complement standardized resuscitation by providing real-time information about circulatory effectiveness, reversible causes, and treatment responses. However, whether physiology-guided interventions improve patient-centered outcomes remains uncertain. This narrative review examines the current evidence and clinical applicability of physiological monitoring during resuscitation, physiology-informed rescue strategies, and individualized post-cardiac arrest care. During cardiopulmonary resuscitation, invasive arterial pressure monitoring, waveform capnography, and echocardiography provide complementary information about the circulation generated by chest compressions and potential mechanisms of resuscitation failure. Although observational and experimental studies support their physiological relevance, no adult diastolic pressure target or pressure-guided vasopressor strategy has been validated to improve survival or neurological recovery. Recent randomized trials of transesophageal echocardiography have demonstrated physiological or procedural effects without establishing clinical benefit. Among rescue strategies, extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation has yielded inconsistent results across randomized trials, with potential benefits dependent on patient selection, intervention timing, and system capabilities. Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta has not improved clinical outcomes in randomized evaluation, while head-up resuscitation remains investigational. Following the return of spontaneous circulation, randomized trials have challenged the benefits of uniformly higher blood pressure and oxygenation targets, mild hypercapnia, and deeper or prolonged temperature control. Individualized approaches incorporating cerebral autoregulation, venous congestion, and cardiopulmonary physiology are physiologically appealing but lack prospective validation. Physiological assessment may complement established resuscitation algorithms by refining clinical decisions during and after cardiac arrest. However, improvements in physiological measurements should not be equated with improved patient outcomes. Future trials should determine whether predefined, physiology-guided treatment strategies improve survival and neurological recovery.

articles.title: Phenotyping of Arrhythmia-induced Cardiomyopathy: From Bench to Bedside and Back.
articles.abstract: Arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy (AIC) is an increasingly recognized and potentially reversible cause or modifier of heart failure. This review summarizes experimental and clinical evidence with a focus on atrial fibrillation (AFib)-induced left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Recent studies demonstrate that AIC extends beyond tachycardia alone and involves rhythm irregularity, loss of atrioventricular synchrony, altered calcium handling, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction and substrate vulnerability. Clinical trials demonstrate the superiority of rhythm control therapy by catheter ablation in patients with AFib and heart failure. Emerging data illustrate the importance of phenotyping of AIC according to myocardial substrate and individual ventricular response to AFib. AIC should be considered as a heterogeneous spectrum. Refined phenotyping may improve prediction of recovery and guide specific and individual therapy.

articles.title: Don't Wait- Ablate! Catheter Ablation in Patients with Advanced Heart Failure and Atrial Fibrillation.
articles.abstract: Heart failure (HF) and atrial fibrillation (AF) frequently coexist and mutually accelerate disease progression through complex hemodynamic, neurohormonal, and structural interactions. Although earlier rhythm-control strategies failed to demonstrate mortality benefit, largely due to limitations of antiarrhythmic drug therapy, catheter ablation has fundamentally altered the therapeutic landscape. The CASTLE-AF trial established catheter ablation as a disease-modifying therapy in patients with AF and HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), demonstrating reductions in mortality and HF hospitalization. More recently, the CASTLE-HTx trial extended these findings to patients with end-stage HF eligible for heart transplantation (HTx) or left ventricular assist device (LVAD) therapy. Catheter ablation has demonstrated a marked reduction in mortality and the need of an urgent HTx, or LVAD implantation compared with medical therapy alone. Subsequent subanalyses further refined risk stratification and identified patient subsets deriving the greatest benefit. Therefore, catheter ablation has received a class 1 recommendation for patients with AF and HFrEF. According to recent clinical evidence supporting early rhythm control through catheter ablation in advanced HF, it leads to a paradigm shift in the management of this high-risk population: in selected patients with AF and advanced HF, clinicians should not delay referral-"Don't wait, ablate."

articles.title: Corrigendum to "Proximal humerus fractures: A review of current management evidence and guidance on contemporary surgical strategies" [Injury 57(11) (2026) 113748].
Chest tube fixation strength depends on suture caliber and fixation technique rather than tube diameter: a biomechanical cadaver study.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Chest tube dislodgement remains a relevant complication in emergency, trauma, and intensive care medicine. In a previous biomechanical study, the Modified Johannesburg technique using Mersilene USP 1 demonstrated superior fixation strength compared with other chest tube fixation techniques. The present study aimed to determine whether suture size, suture material, and chest tube diameter influence fixation strength. A prospective interventional biomechanical cadaveric study was performed using fresh porcine thoracic wall specimens. A total of 320 load-to-failure tests were conducted under standardized laboratory conditions. Two fixation techniques, Modified Johannesburg and Purse String, were compared using two chest tube diameters (20/28 Ch) and four non-absorbable braided suture configurations: Mersilene USP 1, Mersilene USP 2 - 0, Silk USP 1, and Silk USP 2 - 0. Each experimental group consisted of 20 specimens. Specimens were tested in a uniaxial testing machine until construct failure. Force [N] and elongation [mm] at failure were measured. The experiments were videotaped, and the failure mechanism was analyzed. The Modified Johannesburg technique demonstrated significantly higher pull-out forces compared to the Purse String technique (125.0 vs. 66.4 N; p < 0.001), as did larger suture sizes (USP 1 vs. 2 - 0; p < 0.001) and Mersilene compared to Silk (114.6 vs. 76.9 N; p < 0.001). Chest tube size had only a very small and inconsistent effect on pull-out strength. The predominant failure mode was suture rupture (94.7%). Chest tube fixation strength is significantly influenced by fixation technique, suture size, and suture material. The effect of chest tube diameter on fixation strength appeared negligible. The Modified Johannesburg technique, size 1 sutures, and Mersilene material provided superior biomechanical stability. Since failure occurred predominantly by suture rupture, the suture appears to represent the weakest link of the fixation construct.

articles.title: Changes in patellar height following suprapatellar and infrapatellar tibial nailing: a retrospective comparative cohort study.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Patella baja has been described after infrapatellar tibial nailing and may contribute to postoperative knee morbidity; however, whether the nail insertion approach influences postoperative patellar height remains unclear. This study compared longitudinal changes in patellar height (PH) after suprapatellar and infrapatellar intramedullary nailing for tibial shaft fractures. We hypothesized that the suprapatellar approach would better preserve patellar height. A retrospective comparative cohort study included 114 tibial shaft fractures treated with intramedullary nailing between 2016 and 2023, using a suprapatellar (n = 86) or infrapatellar (n = 28) approach. Patellar height was assessed using the Caton-Deschamps Index (CDI) on preoperative and final follow-up radiographs. The primary outcome was the longitudinal change in CDI (ΔCDI). Fracture union, complications, and reoperations were secondary outcomes. The mean reduction in CDI was greater following infrapatellar than suprapatellar nailing (ΔCDI - 0.116 ± 0.173 vs. -0.011 ± 0.107; p = 0.001). After adjustment for baseline CDI and follow-up duration, this association remained significant (adjusted β=-0.055; 95% CI - 0.107 to - 0.004; p = 0.035), although sensitivity analyses showed attenuation after additional adjustment for sex. Fracture union rates were similar between approaches (93.0% vs. 92.9%; p = 0.987), with no statistically significant differences in complications or reoperations. Infrapatellar tibial nailing was associated with a significant postoperative reduction in PH compared with the suprapatellar approach. This association persisted after adjustment for baseline CDI and follow-up duration but was sensitive to additional adjustment for sex. These findings highlight a potential relationship between nail insertion approach and postoperative PH but do not establish an independent effect of surgical approach. Retrospective cohort study (Level III).

articles.title: Intraarticular calcaneal fractures: biomechanical analysis of two fixation constructs.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: The aim of this biomechanical study was to investigate the fixation stability of a small low-profile 2.7 mm variable-angle locking anterolateral calcaneal plate supplemented with two additional independent cortex screws versus a traditional small 3.5 mm locking calcaneal plate in a standardized Sanders IIc fracture model. Sixteen fracture models cocomposed of three polymer blocks (fragments) each and simulating Sanders IIc intra‑articular calcaneal fractures were assigned to two groups. Group 1 (control) received a small 3.5 mm locking calcaneal plate, while Group 2 received a small 2.7 mm variable‑angle locking anterolateral calcaneal plate with two additional independent cortex screws. All constructs were instrumented using prefabricated pilot holes and standardized screw configurations. Biomechanical testing was conducted implementing a 3‑point-bending setup and progressively increasing cyclic loading to failure. Angular interfragmentary movements were quantified via motion tracking along with cycles to clinically relevant failure. Initial stiffness (N/mm) in Group 1 (65.2 ± 34.7) was significantly lower versus Group 2 (232.5 ± 48.6), p = 0.020. Although angular interfragmentary movements around the anteroposterior axis were significantly greater in Group 1 versus Group 2 (p < 0.001), Group 1 demonstrated significantly smaller angular interfragmentary movements around the mediolateral axis for the central-to-posterior and anterior-to-posterior fragment pairs (p ≤ 0.004), while no significant difference between the groups was identified with regard to the central-to-anterior fragment pair (p ≥ 0.377). Cycles and loads (N) to clinically relevant failure in Group 1 (3635 ± 176 and 92.7 ± 3.5) were significantly lower versus Group 2 (17433 ± 628 and 368.7 ± 12.6), p < 0.001. Failure mode in Group 1 involved plate deformation, whereas Group 2 failed through breakage or bending of the independent cortex screws. Biomechanically, fixation implementing a small low-profile 2.7 mm variable-angle locking anterolateral calcaneal plate supplemented with two additional independent cortex screws demonstrated stability comparable to, and in certain respects superior to that achieved with a small 3.5 mm locking calcaneal plate in a standardized Sanders IIc fracture model. However, the findings of this laboratory study do not establish an isolated benefit of the 2.7 mm plate itself, nor do they demonstrate clinical superiority or support alterations to postoperative weight-bearing protocols.

articles.title: Demographic Data Concordance: A Prospective Observational Study of Adolescents, Caregivers, and the Electronic Health Record.
articles.abstract: (1) To measure the concordance of patient demographic data in the electronic health record (EHR); and (2) to determine the level of agreement for patient demographic data between patient report-EHR and patients-caregivers. We conducted a prospective observational survey of 295 patients (age 12 to 17 years) and caregiver dyads presenting to a pediatric emergency department. The primary outcome was concordance, reporting kappa statistics with 95% CI, of caregiver-reported patient race, ethnicity, and sex and the EHR. Secondary outcomes were concordance between: (1) patient report and EHR and (2) patient and caregiver report, including gender identity and preferred language. We surveyed dyads on the perceived impact of demographic characteristics on emergency care and caregivers on preferences for reporting data. For caregiver and EHR report of race, there was substantial agreement for Asian (κ=0.65, 95% CI: 0.44-0.86), Black/African American/African (κ=0.76, 95% CI: 0.66-0.86), and White (κ=0.66, 95% CI: 0.58-0.75) race and moderate agreement for Hispanic/Latino ethnicity (κ=0.53, 95% CI: 0.44-0.61). Patient report and the EHR had similar concordance for race and poor agreement for Hispanic/Latino ethnicity (κ=-0.17, 95% CI: -0.22 to -0.12). For patients and caregivers, there was strong concordance for race, ethnicity, language, and gender identity. Caregivers were more likely than pediatric patients to report that demographic factors affected emergency care. Most caregivers did not have preferences about demographic data reporting methods. Concordance of patient race and ethnicity data in the EHR was variable and should be interpreted cautiously.

Can Emergency Physicians Identify Frozen Tissue on Ultrasound? Implications for Frostbite Management.
articles.abstract: IntroductionFrostbite injuries cause disfigurement and loss of functionality. The role of early imaging in management remains unclear because most modalities require infrastructure that prevents field application. Providers use point-of-care ultrasound to assess a range of soft tissue and musculoskeletal pathologies. The primary objective of this study is to determine the accuracy with which emergency physicians can identify frozen tissue on ultrasound.MethodsThree emergency medicine physicians evaluated whether porcine tissue was frozen or unfrozen by viewing standardized ultrasound clips. The team recorded clips of tissue thawing in a water bath from -10 to +10°C using a handheld ultrasound device. Each physician independently reviewed randomized clips and recorded their assessments. A 2 × 2 table was used to calculate the pooled sensitivity and specificity.ResultsEmergency medicine physicians reviewed 75 clips. They achieved a pooled sensitivity of 76% (95% CI 0.60-0.87) and a specificity of 87% (95% CI 0.68-0.96) for detecting frozen tissue compared with the tissue thermometer as the standard. Their results showed an overall accuracy of 80% (95% CI 0.69-0.88).ConclusionsIn this pilot study, emergency medicine physicians with advanced point-of-care ultrasound training identified frozen tissue on ultrasound 80% of the time. Future research should explore the sonographic features of frozen tissue in cases of frostbite and the test characteristics for sonographers with varying skill levels.

The downside of the pull-up: A 10-year national analysis of emergency department visits, 2015-2024.
articles.abstract: To characterize the epidemiology and clinical patterns of injuries related to pull-up and chin-up bars in a nationally representative emergency department (ED) dataset. Retrospective cross-sectional analysis of the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission National Electronic Injury Surveillance System from January 1, 2015, to December 31, 2024. Cases were identified using product code 3277 with narrative filters for "pull-up," "chin-up," and "doorway bar," excluding barbells and playground equipment. NEISS sampling weights produced national estimates. Annual totals with 95 % confidence intervals were calculated and reported. Injury characteristics were summarized by age group, body region, diagnosis, location, disposition, and a narrative-derived mechanism category (fall, struck by bar, slip or detachment, other). An estimated 40,987 ED visits were attributed to pull-up bar injuries, averaging about 4000 per year, with a peak in 2024 (5421; 95 % CI, 5315-5527). Patients were predominantly male (66.1 %) with a bimodal age distribution centered on children 5-14 years and adults 18-34 years. Craniofacial trauma predominated, with head and face together comprising nearly one-half of presentations, followed by upper-extremity involvement, including shoulder, wrist, and forearm. Laceration, internal head injury, and fracture were the leading diagnoses, with sprain or strain and contusion also frequent. Most incidents occurred in the home, and 93.8 % of patients were treated and released. Falls were the most common mechanism, followed by struck-by events and a subset explicitly involving bar slip or detachment. Pull-up bar injuries constitute a consistent national burden of craniofacial and upper-extremity trauma concentrated in youth and young adults, largely managed nonoperatively in acute care settings. Improved recognition of exercise-associated injury mechanisms may assist diagnostic accuracy and reduce the burden on emergency and orthopedic services.

articles.title: How the cause of surgical delay affects mortality in fragility hip fractures: A cohort study.
articles.abstract: Prompt surgery for fragility hip fractures is a cornerstone of care and a key metric within the Best Practice Tariff (BPT) in the United Kingdom. Yet, since 2011, time to theatre has steadily increased, BPT adherence has fallen, and paradoxically, mortality has reduced. It is still unclear if surgical delay is an independent predictor of mortality. Emerging evidence suggests that the causes of surgical delays may be more important determinants of mortality than the delay itself. A cohort study of 1769 hip fracture patients above the age of 60 was conducted in a single centre in England. This study collected demographic data, timing to theatre (<36 h vs ≥36 h), reasons for any delays, 30-day mortality and 1-year mortality between March 2020 and December 2024. The most common cause of delay was insufficient theatre capacity (N = 365, 20.6%), followed by delays awaiting medical stabilisation (N = 102, 5.8%). Age (Χ2 71.638 p < 0.001), ASA grade (Χ2 37.045 p < 0.001), sex (Χ2 27.721 p < 0.001), pre-admission residence (Χ2 36.772 p < 0.001), and reason for delay (Χ2 27.495 p = 0.007) were significant predictors of mortality. Delays due solely because of theatre unavailability did not increase 30-day (OR 0.784 p = 0.398) or 1-year mortality (OR 1.123 p = 0.474). In contrast, delays due to medical optimisation were associated with markedly higher 30-day (OR 3.573, p < 0.001) and 1-year mortality (OR 2.144, p = 0.005). While early surgery remains beneficial, patients delayed solely due to administrative reasons did not demonstrate an associated increase in mortality. Mortality associated with operative delay was primarily associated amongst patients with concurrent acute illnesses and co-morbidities, independently increasing risk. To improve mortality, the focus must remain on pre-operative optimisation and robust orthogeriatric assessment, rather than surgical timing alone. Future iterations of the BPT may benefit from incorporating the cause of delay and physiological risk stratification to surgical timing targets to better align national incentives with clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Clinical significance of "complex" multimorbidity in hospitalised adult patients.
articles.abstract: The term "complex multimorbidity" lacks universal consensus and its relevance remains unclear. We aimed to assess the prevalence of complex multimorbidity and its association with major healthcare outcomes. This was a prospective, single-centre study (internal medicine ward). We collected sociodemographic and clinical data and we categorised patients into non-overlapping categories, namely no multimorbidity, basic multimorbidity (two or more chronic conditions, with no qualifiers of complex multimorbidity), or complex multimorbidity ([a], ≥ 3 chronic conditions from ≥ 3 different body systems; [b], at least one physical and one mental condition; and [c], being ≥ 65 years old with ≥ 4 chronic conditions, including vision/hearing problems). The prevalence of multimorbidity sub-definitions and their association with major outcomes were assessed. Among 1415 patients (median age 80 years, IQR 69-86, F:M 1.15:1), multimorbidity (96.2%) and complex multimorbidity (93.8%) were highly prevalent. Complex multimorbidity was associated with older age, female sex (b 62.3% and c 62.4%), low income (b, 55.3%), and frailty (c, 94.1%), and significantly correlated with 12-month readmission to ward/emergency department, 12-month outpatient visits, and prescription changes. At multivariable analysis, complex multimorbidity a (OR 2.97; 95% CI 1.46-6.06; p = 0.003) and b (OR 2.98; 95% CI 1.37-6.47; p = 0.006) were associated with polypharmacy at discharge. Five-year mortality increased from no multimorbidity (0.076 per 100 person-months) to complex multimorbidity, being higher in complex a (1.947 per 100 person-months), b (2.428 per 100 person-months), and c (2.284 per 100 person-months). Complex multimorbidity provides meaningful clinical information in internal medicine. Further studies are needed to validate these observations.

articles.title: Mimics and Chameleons: A Patient with Accidental Hypothermia and Myocardial Infarction.
articles.abstract: BackgroundAccidental hypothermia is an unintentional drop in core temperature below 35 °C, typically resulting from exposure to cold environmental conditions. Clinical presentations may vary widely depending on the severity of hypothermia and the presence of coexisting conditions complicating diagnosis and treatment. We report a case of accidental hypothermia caused by environmental exposure and associated with cardiogenic shock from a myocardial infarction with complete heart block.Case PresentationA group of ski tourers found a 62-y-old male skier at 3000 m in severe distress with abdominal pain, shivering, and profound exhaustion. On arrival at a mountain hut, he was agitated, then became unconscious and bradycardic with a weak femoral pulse. Once advanced medical equipment reached the hut, a 12-lead electrocardiogram showed an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) with complete third-degree atrioventricular block and a ventricular escape rhythm. The first measurable axillary temperature was 32.2 °C. Consciousness progressively improved, but bradycardia persisted during rewarming. The patient was evacuated 6 h after the diagnosis of acute STEMI. He underwent percutaneous coronary intervention and was successfully treated with a stent.ConclusionsThis case illustrates that hypothermia and environmental factors can complicate the diagnosis of atypical presentations of life-threatening conditions, such as STEMI, and how unexpected clinical findings not fully explained by hypothermia may indicate the presence of an underlying condition. In such situations, hypothermia staging systems should be used with caution. Early electrocardiography, awareness of cognitive biases, and the use of safe rewarming practices are essential to ensure timely diagnosis and prevent complications.

articles.title: Exposomic Determinants in Heart Failure Among Older Adults - Mechanistic Links, Clinical Evidence, and Future Perspectives.
articles.abstract: Heart failure (HF) in older adults emerges from the interplay between biological aging and the totality of environmental and behavioural exposures conceptualized as the exposome. Traditional cardiovascular risk factors and intrinsic cardiac pathology only partially explain HF burden, as chronic exposures to air pollution, traffic noise, temperature extremes, toxic metals and chemicals, artificial light at night, and adverse social environments, along with low greenness and walkability, substantially influence HF incidence, decompensations, and prognosis in older patients with multiple comorbidities. Recently, epidemiological studies have associated many of the exposomic factors with HF incidence and morbidity. Age‑related impairments of the myocardium and vasculature make them particularly vulnerable to external stressors. Mechanistically, aging, HF, and environmental factors converge on shared pathways including, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammaging, impaired autophagy and proteostasis, genomic and epigenetic alterations, cellular senescence, dysregulated neurohormonal and circadian signalling, and fibrosis with maladaptive remodelling. Through these mechanisms exposome chronically accelerates cardiovascular aging and lowers the threshold for HF onset and progression. This review considers a shift from an organ‑centred view of HF in older adults to a systems‑level, life‑course perspective that explicitly incorporates exposomic determinants, and argues that reducing harmful exposures while promoting green space, physical activity, walkability, and healthy dietary patterns should be integral to HF prevention and management strategies in aging societies.

articles.title: The blunt truth: The role of marijuana in PTSD after intentional traumatic injury.
articles.abstract: Survivors of interpersonal violence experience high rates of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and rates of marijuana use are rising among young adults. There is however, limited understanding of marijuana use patterns among survivors of interpersonal violence with PTSD. We evaluated relationships between PTSD and marijuana use following injury and hypothesized that PTSD-positive patients would report elevated follow-up marijuana use. Between 10/2019 and 7/1/2024, we prospectively collected data on patient demographics, PTSD, substance use (including marijuana), and PROMIS-29 quality of life domains for adult trauma patients admitted to an urban, academic, level-1 trauma center. Participants were screened at baseline and at 6- or 12-month follow-up. Injury characteristics were collected from the institutional trauma registry. Among the intentionally injured, we compared patients by follow-up PTSD screening results. We excluded patients who screened positive for PTSD at baseline. Using multivariable logistic regression we assessed relationships between follow-up PTSD and marijuana use, including demographic and injury characteristics as covariates. Our primary outcome was dichotomized follow-up marijuana use. Of 105 participants injured by intentional trauma with complete follow-up data, 69 screened negative for PTSD at baseline and therefore were included in this analysis. Patients who screened positive for PTSD at follow-up had greater marijuana use at baseline (29% vs 3%, p = 0.002) and follow-up (42% vs 13%, p = 0.007), and worse PROMIS-29 scores in all domains (p ≤ 0.01), compared to PTSD-negative patients. In multivariable analysis, screening positive for PTSD was associated with 7.1 times greater odds of marijuana use at follow-up (p = 0.007, CI:1.7, 29.5). PTSD and marijuana use were closely associated in survivors of interpersonal violence. Screening efforts should account for marijuana use specifically. Routine screening for marijuana use could improve recognition of psychological challenges after trauma and could help identify patients at risk for development of PTSD. Level III, prognostic/epidemiological.

A Case Report of Lyme Carditis Presenting as New-Onset Atrial Flutter in the Emergency Department.
articles.abstract: Lyme disease (LD) is the most common vector-borne disease in the United States and has several well-known pathologic sequelae if not treated, including third-degree atrioventricular block. However, an association between Lyme carditis and atrial arrhythmias has been described in some cardiology literature but has not been reported in emergency medicine or wilderness medicine literature. This case report describes an older adult with new-onset atrial flutter with rapid ventricular rate in the setting of early disseminated LD, who ultimately was treated with antibiotics, had resolution of atrial flutter, and has had no recurrence. As cardiac inflammation secondary to organ infection may manifest as multiple forms of arrhythmia, this case report highlights the importance of considering LD as a differential diagnosis when treating tick-exposed patients with new cardiac arrhythmias, including atrial flutter.

articles.title: UTILITY OF INDOCYANINE GREEN FLUORESCENCE IMAGING IN BURN MANAGEMENT: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: The implementation of near-infrared fluorescence (NIRF) imaging using indocyanine green (ICG) has seen a rising implementation in burn care in recent years, with expanding clinical indications and increasing evidence supporting its use. A systematic review was carried out following PRISMA guidelines, employing PubMed, Web of Science, CINAHL, and EMBASE databases to locate studies on the perioperative use of ICG in burn patients. Two independent reviewers assessed all articles for eligibility based on predefined inclusion criteria. Extracted data included study characteristics, patient demographics, clinical indications, ICG dosing regimens, administration timing, and reported perioperative outcomes. A total of 12 studies enrolling 204 burn patients, published between 1995 and 2025, were included for qualitative synthesis. Of these, 7 (58.3%) were prospective, single-center experimental studies; 3 (25%) were prospective, multicenter, blinded trials; 1 (8.3%) was a retrospective study; and 1 (8.3%) was a case series. The primary clinical uses of ICG in burn management included: assessment of burn depth reported in 6 studies, intraoperative delineation of necrotic tissue requiring excision in 3 studies, utility of ICG in liver function measurement in 2 studies and another research analyzed the estimation of plasma volume in burn patients. ICG fluorescence imaging is a promising adjunctive tool for burn assessment, particularly in identifying non-perfused tissue. It enhances the ability to accurately assess burn depth and helps to determine surgical margins during burn excision. Furthermore, ICG pharmacokinetics may provide insight into liver involvement and prognostic outlook in severe burn cases. However, its current role remains complementary to clinical evaluation. Further standardized and high-quality studies are required to define its diagnostic accuracy and clinical impact.

articles.title: Bridging the Evidence Gap: A Call to Action for Anticoagulation Research in Pediatric Burned Patients on Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Although early extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) improves respiratory complications in unburned populations, it remains a rarely utilized rescue therapy in pediatric burn care, averaging just 3 to 6 cases annually worldwide despite a promising 53-62% survival rate. This underutilization stems from a profound therapeutic paradox: the high bleeding risks and need for coagulation inherent to burn wounds with necessary surgical debridement directly conflict with the systemic anticoagulation required to prevent ECMO circuit thrombosis. Importantly, emerging evidence demonstrates that systemic anticoagulation may not be an absolute requirement for veno-venous ECMO. Despite this, no guidance exists for anticoagulation management specifically in pediatric burned patients. A scoping review spanning three databases identified no studies describing a coagulation strategy developed or validated for this population. Addressing this evidence gap is essential to safely transition ECMO from a late rescue modality to an earlier, evidence-based intervention capable of reducing mortality in this patient population. We therefore call for (1) a multicenter collaboration to aggregate sufficient case volume for meaningful analysis; (2) a prospective collection of serial viscoelastic and conventional coagulation data in pediatric burned patients on ECMO to characterize the temporal evolution of coagulopathy on circuit; and (3) the development and validation of coagulation management protocols tailored to this population. Until such evidence exists, pediatric burned patients will continue to be denied a therapy that offers meaningful survival-not because ECMO does not work-but because we have not yet determined how best to manage coagulation while on circuit.

articles.title: Understanding Functional Recovery in Burn Survivors Aged 80 Years and Older: A Burn Model System Study.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: The global demographic shift toward an aging population is transforming burn care, yet the "oldest old" (adults ≥80 years) remain poorly understood. Standard geriatric guidelines are not specific to this subgroup, a group exhibiting unique physiological needs and vulnerabilities. We conducted a retrospective analysis of the Burn Model System (BMS) National Database for adults aged 80 years or older (N=104).1 Physical Function, Ability to Participate in Social Roles, and Pain Interference were assessed at 6 and 12 months post-burn and compared to pre-burn and US population norm (aged ≥75 years) data. Despite sustaining moderate injuries (Mean TBSA: 11.7%), our cohort required prolonged hospitalization (Mean: 26.9 days). We identified a functional recovery paradox: while Physical Function scores were low (40.1) at 12 months, Social Roles scores were average (50.0 at 6 months and 51.9 at 12 months). Notably, referral to inpatient rehabilitation (IPR) was highly variable (8.6% to 42.1%) and correlated strongly with social support; patients living alone were three times less likely to receive IPR than those with co-habitants (17.7% vs 61.7%). In conclusion, burn survivors aged 80 years and older face persistent reduction in physical function but demonstrate resilience in maintaining social roles, suggesting that slow physical recovery does not preclude quality of life. Prolonged acute hospitalizations and variable IPR access highlight the need for geriatric-specific guidelines to address the unique physiological, social, and systemic barriers that challenge the "oldest old."

articles.title: Clinical outcomes of combined MPFL-reconstruction with MPTL-augmenting patellar distalization using hamstring autograft versus isolated MPFL in adolescents with patella alta: a retrospective comparative study.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Patella alta is a major risk factor for recurrent patellar dislocation in adolescents. This study aimed to compare the clinical outcomes of isolated medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) reconstruction with those of MPFL reconstruction augmented by medial patellotibial ligament (MPTL)-distalization, both using a semitendinosus hamstring autograft, in adolescent patients with patella alta. A retrospective cohort study was conducted on 28 adolescent patients (mean age 11.2 ± 1.6 years; 9 males, 19 females) treated for recurrent patellar dislocation between May 2020 and July 2025. All patients had patella alta (Caton-Deschamps index > 1.2) and a history of at least one dislocation, with varying degrees of trochlear dysplasia (Dejour types A-B). All patients underwent MPFL reconstruction using a semitendinosus hamstring autograft harvested with preservation of its native distal tibial insertion, fixed via a single oblique transpatellar tunnel and femoral interference-screw fixation proximal to the distal femoral physis. Group A (n=14) underwent isolated MPFL reconstruction. Group B (n=14) underwent the same MPFL reconstruction with an additional MPTL-augmenting patellar distalization step using the same graft, secured by trans-osseous periosteal suture at the lateral patella. Surgical techniques emphasized physeal spare during reconstruction. Preoperative and postoperative assessments included the Kujala score, Lysholm score, Caton-Deschamps index, and sulcus angle. Follow-up averaged 12- 24 months. CT was performed using a low-dose pediatric protocol specifically for TT-TG measurement and trochlear bony morphology; MRI was used for soft-tissue and cartilage assessment. Group assignment was not randomized; patients with more pronounced patella alta and higher-grade clinical instability were preferentially treated with the combined procedure. Both groups showed significant improvements in functional scores. In Group (A), Kujala scores improved from 59.3 ± 8.3 to 84.3 ± 5.1, and Lysholm scores from 50.3 ± 7.5 to 74.7 ± 9.3. Caton-Deschamps index decreased from 1.27 to 1.20. In Group (B), Kujala scores improved from 56.2 ± 7.4 to 88.9 ± 4.5, and Lysholm scores from 51.4 ± 7.6 to 87.4 ± 6.2. Caton-Deschamps index decreased from 1.28 to 1.11, indicating better patellar height correction. Complications occurred in 36% of Group A and 21% of Group B. Recurrent instability occurred in 2 patients (14%) in Group A and 1 patient (7%) in Group B; all were subluxation episodes managed non-operatively, and no revision surgery was required. This study demonstrated that MPFL reconstruction with MPTL-augmenting patellar distalization using a hamstring autograft yields greater functional improvements, superior patella alta correction, and fewer complications compared to isolated MPFL reconstruction in adolescents with recurrent patellar instability. Retrospective comparative study; level IV. Clinical trial number: not applicable. This study is a retrospective comparative cohort study and does not meet the definition of a clinical trial as per the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) guidelines, as it involves retrospective analysis of routinely collected clinical data without prospective intervention or randomization.

articles.title: Health economic evaluation of polytrauma treatment in the current aG-DRG system - Results of a Level I Trauma Center.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Resource-intensive polytrauma care is associated with high treatment and readiness costs and poses a financial challenge for hospitals. The aim of this retrospective single-center study of the years 2020 to 2022 was to analyze polytrauma reimbursements and costs. Based on billing and clinical data of 201 polytrauma cases from a German University Hospital and Level I Trauma Center, revenues and costs of the eleven MDC 21 A polytrauma DRGs were analyzed. Ratios of the revenue in relation to LOS, ventilation hours, OR time and implant costs as well as personnel costs were calculated. Contribution margins were determined as an upper-bound estimate. DRG reimbursement was highest for the most severely injured patients (50,852 €, DRG W36Z). It was lowest for patients who died within five days (2,214 €, DRG W60Z) or without surgeries (4,056 €, DRG W61B). The contribution margin was also highest for the most severely injured patients (52,775 €, DRG W36Z). Revenues in relation to ICU LOS (3,455 €/day, DRG W36Z) and ventilation time (238 €/hour, DRG W01B) were lowest for the most severe polytraumas. Regarding OR time and implant costs, reimbursement was lowest for injuries of the spine, pelvis and extremities with 62 €/min (DRG W02B) and 5 €/€ (DRG W02A). Treatment of polytrauma patients with long ICU stay, extended mechanical ventilation and multiple injuries of the extremities, pelvis and spine is not adequately reflected by the current per-case reimbursement in relation to the resources used (ICU days, ventilation hours, OR time and implant costs).

articles.title: Quantitative decision-support strategies to enhance emergency medical service accessibility in high-risk freeway tunnels.
articles.abstract: Crashes inside road tunnels often result in more severe outcomes due to spatial constraints that delay prehospital emergency medical services (EMS) access. Emergency evacuation facilities, such as cross passages and emergency parking areas, are critical for ensuring timely EMS response during traffic congestion caused by in-tunnel crashes. This study presents a quantitative approach to develop targeted strategies for enhancing such facilities to improve EMS accessibility in tunnels. Nationwide in-tunnel crash data from Korean freeways over a four-year period were analyzed, and the limited number of severe crash cases was addressed using SMOTE-based data augmentation to balance severity levels in the prediction model. A SHAP-based XGBoost classifier was applied to identify the influence of key features related to EMS accessibility and emergency evacuation facilities on crash severity. The results showed that crashes occurring more than 1 km from the tunnel entrance and EMS response coverage within a 10-15 km range have a significant impact on increasing crash severity. The presence of emergency cross passages, three or more lanes, emergency parking areas, and properly spaced CCTV installations were found to help reduce crash severity. Based on these findings, tunnels with particularly limited EMS accessibility were prioritized, and tailored facility improvement measures were proposed. This study provides quantitative evidence to guide cost-effective upgrades of tunnel emergency evacuation facilities, enhancing prehospital EMS accessibility and emergency preparedness. The proposed methodology can also support decision-making on implementing road tunnel safety improvement policies.

articles.title: Community Paramedics Addressing the Evolving Opioid Crisis: A Case Series Addressing the Kratom Derivatives 7-Hydroxymitragynine and MGM-15.
articles.abstract: Concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) and dihydro-7-hydroxymitragynine (MGM-15) are derived from the primary psychoactive alkaloid in kratom, and until recently were sold over the counter with kratom products. These highly potent kratom derivatives can produce opioid-like dependence, but evidence around prehospital treatment of 7-OH and MGM-15 withdrawal symptoms remains limited. This case series assesses two cases of community paramedics (CPs) providing treatment and linkage to care for individuals in acute opioid withdrawal from 7-OH and MGM-15. In our first case a 74-year-old individual called 9-1-1 experiencing acute opioid-like withdrawal symptoms after abruptly discontinuing over the counter 7-OH following six months of progressively escalating use. Connection was made with a prehospital buprenorphine program (PBAP) and the CP administered 24mg of buprenorphine and expedited connection to outpatient treatment with medication for opioid use disorder (MOUD). Our second case involved a 38-year-old individual who called a CP requesting expedited linkage to MOUD following a period of escalating use of 7-OH and MGM-15. This patient was linked to MOUD treatment within 48 hours of contacting the CP and required 32mg/8mg of buprenorphine/naloxone to treat severe opioid withdrawal symptoms after discontinued use of MGM-15 tablets. Both patients were retained in MOUD treatment at 30 days. These cases describe use of CP-based PBAPs addressing severe 7-OH withdrawal and expediting treatment to outpatient MOUD, highlighting that concentrated over the counter 7-OH products can produce physical opioid dependence leading to opioid use disorder, and requiring full-dose buprenorphine induction which may be considered within existing prehospital opioid withdrawal treatment protocols. Additional research is necessary to characterize withdrawal from concentrated 7-OH products and to determine implications for PBAP protocols and 7-OH dosing in the United States.

articles.title: Prehospital antibiotics and 28-day mortality in sepsis: where does the adjusted benefit come from?
Economic evaluations in emergency medicine: a 25-year systematic review of patient-level cost-effectiveness analyses (2000-2025).
articles.journal: European journal of emergency medicine : official journal of the European Society for Emergency Medicine
articles.abstract: Emergency departments (EDs) face rising demand and resource constraints. Cost-effectiveness analyses (CEAs) can inform resource allocation, but patient-level CEAs in emergency care remain methodologically heterogeneous. This review aimed to identify and describe patient-level CEAs in emergency care between 2000 and 2025, appraise their methodological quality, and explore temporal trends and evidence gaps. This systematic review was reported according to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020. PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, CENTRAL, and gray literature were searched for patient-level CEAs of clinical or organizational interventions across prehospital, ED, and postemergency settings. Data were synthesized narratively across key methodological domains. Methodological quality of the economic evaluations was assessed using the quality of health economic studies (QHES) instrument. Descriptive and exploratory analyses were performed. Forty-seven studies were identified, of which 96% were conducted in EDs. Infectious diseases and ED crowding were the most addressed topics, followed by cardiovascular conditions and trauma, although a broad range of issues was covered. Studies were mainly conducted in high-income countries and evaluated organizational or diagnostic interventions. Healthcare system or hospital perspectives and short time horizons predominated. QHES scores were moderate-to-high (mean: 80.0, SD: 9.2, range: 56-96), with substantial variability and only a weak exploratory temporal trend toward higher scores. Prehospital and postemergency settings were underrepresented. Patient-level CEAs in emergency medicine are increasing, with many studies achieving high QHES scores, but remain heterogeneous in scope and methods. This review highlights the range of interventions evaluated and the methodological features relevant to interpreting economic evidence in emergency care.

articles.title: Patterns, and outcomes of airbag -related penetrating injuries: a retrospective analysis from a level 1 trauma center.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: The deployment of defective airbag inflators can generate high-velocity metallic fragments that cause face, neck or chest penetrating injuries with potentially lethal consequences. This study aimed to describe the injury patterns, management, and outcomes of suspected airbag-related penetrating injuries (ARPI) among patients in a Middle Eastern country. A retrospective observational study of patients presenting with penetrating injuries suspected of being related to defective airbag deployment. Data were obtained from the Qatar National Trauma Registry (QNTR), electronic medical records, emergency medical services (EMS), emergency department (ED), and Mortuary. Data were collected and analyzed descriptively. A total of 16 patients had suspected ARPIs between April 2019 and February 2026. The mean age was 33.1 ± 8.3 years, and 93.8% were male. Metallic foreign bodies (FBs) from airbag inflator fragmentation were documented in 11/16 (68.8%) patients by imaging, and surgical removal while in 4/16 patients there were only entry-exit wounds after deployment of airbags following car crash. In one case, airbag deployed while mechanic was repairing a car steering wheel. Penetrating neck (43.8%), thoracic (31.3%), and maxillofacial injuries (31.3%), predominantly mandibular fractures, were most common. Surgical intervention was required in 11 (68.8%) patients and 7/16 required intensive care unit admissions. Five patients died (31.3%), including one at the scene (transported directly by the EMS, no CPR, and moved to the hospital mortuary), two died at the ED after unsuccessful CPR and two died during the hospital course (one presented with cardiac arrest and died on the sixth day and the other one required prolonged ECMO for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and died after 4 months). Airbag inflator rupture can produce serious injury patterns resembling patterns of ballistic trauma, characterized by penetrating neck wounds, maxillofacial fractures and thoracic injuries. These injuries are potentially associated with high mortality, surgical intervention, and critical care utilization. The full extent of these injuries is undetermined as some victims may have simply died at the scene without the benefit of trauma center evaluation or post-mortem examination.

articles.title: Hospital Specialization and Geographic Access as Determinants of Pediatric Emergency Mortality: A Nationwide Multilevel Study in South Korea.
articles.abstract: To examine individual, hospital, and community-level determinants of in-hospital mortality-defined as death during the emergency department visit or after hospitalization at the same hospital-among critically ill pediatric emergency patients in South Korea. We analyzed data from the National Emergency Department Information System, comprising 26,206 pediatric patients (aged ≤18 y, triage levels 1 to 2) at emergency medical centers in 2021, using multilevel logistic regression. The null model confirmed substantial between-hospital [intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC)=0.17] and between-community (ICC=0.01) variation, justifying the multilevel approach. Overall, in-hospital mortality was 2.3%. At the individual level, compared with self-transport, patients arriving by 119 ambulance (OR=2.73, 95% CI: 1.85-4.05) and private ambulance patients (OR=3.14, 95% CI: 1.72-5.73) had higher odds. Intentional and unintentional injuries showed 2.06-fold and 2.97-fold higher odds versus noninjury, respectively. Consciousness level showed a dose-response association (coma: OR=228.64). Severe illness was associated with a 4.94-fold higher odds ratio. At the hospital level, higher critically ill proportions were associated with lower mortality (≥10%: OR=0.43), while hospitals with ≥45 combined pediatric and neonatal intensive care beds had higher odds (OR=2.43), likely reflecting case-mix concentration. At the community level, metropolitan cities showed higher odds (OR=1.64), while a higher Timely Relevance Index (TRI; percentage of residents accessing care within 60 min) was associated with lower mortality (≥95%: OR=0.55). Pediatric emergency mortality was associated with factors across all 3 levels. Risk-adjusted performance metrics are needed for tiered systems, and timely geographic access supports distributed initial stabilization capacity.

articles.title: Low-Titer O+ Whole Blood Implementation in the EMS System for Metropolitan Oklahoma City and Tulsa: Significance, Success, & Sharing Lessons Learned.
articles.abstract: Over 300 emergency medical services (EMS) organizations across the United States have implemented transfusion programs for traumatic injuries using packed red blood cells, platelets, plasma, or whole blood before hospital arrival. Beginning in December of 2022, the EMS System for Metropolitan Oklahoma City (OKC) and Tulsa began carrying low-titer O-positive whole blood (LTOWB) for adult patients in traumatic hemorrhagic shock, specifically those exhibiting elevated shock indexes. We aim to describe establishing our prehospital LTOWB program and its first two years of operations across OKC and Tulsa. We used an observational study design and retrospective descriptive analysis of patients receiving LTOWB by paramedic transfusion from the Emergency Medical Services Authority Ambulance Service, Oklahoma City Fire Department, or Tulsa Fire Department between December 1, 2022, and February 1, 2025. Descriptive analysis and univariate logistic regression quantify the relationship of patient characteristics against survival to hospital arrival and survival to hospital discharge outcomes. Penetrating trauma was the most common mechanism of injury recorded for patients receiving EMS LTOWB (71.6%). Following LTOWB transfusion, prehospital vital signs (systolic blood pressure, heart rate, and shock index) significantly improved (p < 0.05). Systolic blood pressure improvement conferred 9.7 times greater odds of survival to hospital arrival (95% CL 1.6-58.6). Occurrence of prehospital traumatic arrest was significantly related to lower odds of survival to hospital arrival and survival to hospital discharge (OR 0.01 and OR 0.03, respectively). Transfusion of LTOWB in a large, urban EMS system in the Southwestern United States confers a positive benefit to patients with measurable improvement in median systolic blood pressure, heart rate, and shock index. Continuous review of cases and misses empowered our system in dynamic protocol adjustments to best meet our population's needs. Patients often had secondary deterioration during transit, illustrating that blood transfusion "bought" temporary time during transport of critically injured patients to definitive care.

articles.title: Pediatric Rural Interfacility Transfers by Emergency Medical Services.
articles.abstract: Interfacility transports (IFTs) are critical for the care of pediatric patients in the United States (US), particularly in rural areas that may have limited pediatric specialty resources. Given the paucity of data describing rural pediatric IFTs, we aimed to characterize pediatric rural IFTs in the US. We conducted a retrospective, observational study using the 2023 National Emergency Medical Services Information System dataset. Rural IFTs involving patients aged ≥1 day to <18 years were included and stratified into the following age groups: infant (1 day to <1 year), toddler (1-2 years), preschooler (3-5 years), young child (6-11 years), and teenager (12 to <18 years). Using descriptive statistics, we analyzed patient demographics, clinical characteristics, emergency medical services (EMS) transport characteristics, medications, procedures, and transport time intervals. We identified 29,992 rural pediatric IFTs (median age: 8 years [IQR: 2-14 years]; 52.9% male). Teenagers represented the largest age group transferred (38.8%). Respiratory diseases (12.3%) were the most common primary impression overall, whereas psychiatric and behavioral health conditions predominated among teenagers. Ground transport accounted for most IFTs (79.4%), and advanced life support units were the most common transport level of care (62.7%). Infants demonstrated the highest proportion of specialty critical care transports (32.1%) and longer median response and total call intervals across transport modalities compared with older age groups. Younger children more commonly received respiratory-focused medications and procedures, whereas teenagers more frequently received pain management and sedative medications. Nearly 30,000 pediatric rural IFTs occurred in 2023, with substantial age-related differences in clinical presentations, transport characteristics, and EMS interventions. Infants more frequently required specialty critical care transport and experienced longer transport intervals, whereas psychiatric and behavioral health conditions represented a substantial proportion of adolescent transfers. These findings underscore the importance of pediatric-focused EMS preparedness, transport readiness, and clinical training initiatives to support safe rural pediatric interfacility care.

articles.title: Prognostic value of early point-of-care blood gas analysis in critically ill non-trauma patients.
articles.abstract: Critically ill non-trauma patients treated in the emergency department have a high risk of in-hospital mortality. While point-of-care diagnostics such as blood gas analysis are established tools for urgent management, data on their prognostic value in this specific patient cohort remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate whether initial blood gas parameters are independently associated with in-hospital mortality in critically ill non-trauma patients. This retrospective cohort study included adult critically ill non-trauma patients treated in the emergency department of a German university hospital. Initial blood gas parameters and clinical data were analyzed using univariate and multivariable logistic regression to assess their association with in-hospital mortality. Of 879 screened patients, 542 met the inclusion criteria. In-hospital mortality was 20% (n = 110). In addition to older age and out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, anemia (hemoglobin < 12 g/dL; OR of 2.07, 95% CI 1.20-3.58; p = 0.009), acidosis (pH < 7.35; OR 2.26, 95% CI 1.09-4.95; p = 0.033) and hypobicarbonatemia (< 22 mmol/L; OR 2.79, 95% CI 1.42-5.69; p = 0.004) were independently associated with in-hospital mortality. The association for hyperlactatemia was borderline (> 2.2 mmol/L; OR 1.85, 95% CI 0.93-3.77; p = 0.08). Multivariate analysis did not reveal significant associations between other electrolyte imbalances and in-hospital mortality in this cohort. In this retrospective cohort, the presence of anemia, acidosis or hypobicarbonatemia on admission to the resuscitation room were independently associated with an elevated risk of in-hospital mortality in critically ill non-trauma patients. These readily available point-of-care parameters may support early risk stratification. Prospective studies are needed to validate these findings.

articles.title: [Clinical Decision Unit in the emergency department-a systems analysis of a clinical decision model for hospital admission management].
articles.abstract: Observation units are an established component of modern emergency departments. However, limited data are available on the operational, governance, and staffing concepts underlying their performance. To describe and evaluate the Clinical Decision Unit model of a university interdisciplinary emergency department. This retrospective cohort study included all adult nontrauma patients treated in 2024. Organizational structure, care pathways, resource utilization, and outcomes were analyzed. A simulation estimated additional inpatient bed demand in a hypothetical scenario without the Clinical Decision Unit model. Among 17,001 patients, 10,327 (60.7%) received inpatient management within the Clinical Decision Unit model. Of these, 3880 (37.6%) completed their care within the emergency department, whereas 6447 (62.4%) were transferred to an inpatient specialty ward. Patients receiving definitive care within the emergency department remained for a median of 9.6 h and required comparable diagnostic and therapeutic resources. In the hypothetical scenario without the Clinical Decision Unit model, an additional 5485 bed-days would have been required on inpatient wards; after accounting for the bed capacity required within the emergency department, the net capacity difference was 4191 bed-days, equivalent to a mean of 11.5 beds. A structured Clinical Decision Unit model can complete inpatient care within the emergency department and preserve inpatient capacity. Experienced interprofessional teams, clear clinical decision-making responsibility, and appropriate emergency care infrastructure are essential prerequisites.
